subject: Decision: VPC peering vs PrivateLink vs Site-to-site VPN for private deployment handoff
messages:
From: Alice Kruger <alice.kruger@acmecorp.com>
To: sergio_alvarez@redwood.ai
Cc: netops-team@acmecorp.com, dpo@acmecorp.com
Date: 2027-11-03T08:12:00-07:00
Subject: Request: recommended connectivity pattern for private deployment

Hi Sergio,

Quick context: Acme is evaluating a private deployment of Redwood inside our VPC for a regulated analytics workload. NetOps and DPO are concerned about maintaining strong security posture while preserving client IP visibility and keeping predictable tail latency.

We'd like Redwood's recommendation between three handoff options: VPC peering, AWS PrivateLink (interface VPC endpoints), and a site-to-site VPN to a co-lo gateway (for now VPN over IPSec). Key constraints:
- Preserve originating client IPs to pass to downstream audit logs where possible
- No additional public egress (we prefer traffic to remain inside Acme/Redwood network boundary)
- SLA requirement: 99.9% availability, p99 latency < 120ms for peak flows
- Budget sensitivity: link egress costs and cross-account data charges matter

Can you outline tradeoffs and one recommended path + an ops failover plan? I attached our initial matrix and the DPO questionnaire.

Thanks,
Alice
Alice Kruger
Head of Infrastructure, AcmeCorp

Attachments: acme_redwood_connectivity_matrix.xlsx (spreadsheet), acme_security_questionnaire.pdf (survey)

From: Sergio Alvarez <sergio_alvarez@redwood.ai>
To: Alice Kruger <alice.kruger@acmecorp.com>
Cc: kimberly_park@redwood.ai, ben_carter@redwood.ai
Date: 2027-11-03T11:05:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Request: recommended connectivity pattern for private deployment

Alice — thanks for the clear brief and the attachments. I pulled together an initial recommendation and a short tradeoff summary. High-level answer: for Acme's constraints I recommend starting with PrivateLink (interface endpoints) + a negotiated egress tier for high-throughput paths, with VPC peering as a low-latency fallback in the same region where we can accept cross-account route limitations. Site-to-site VPN should be treated as an emergency fallback or for on-prem segments that cannot use cloud-native endpoints.

Why PrivateLink first (short):
- Security isolation: interface endpoints terminate inside Acme's VPC and allow us to accept inbound TLS connections from Acme without exposing public IPs.
- No SNAT on Redwood side when using NLB-backed PrivateLink with proxy-preserve-client-ip configured — client IP preservation is achievable with the right proxy config (we'll document runbook steps).
- Predictable networking boundary and IAM-based access controls are simpler for your auditors (DPO liked this pattern in other engagements).

Why VPC peering as fallback (short):
- Lowest possible intra-region network path and avoids NATting, but requires route table management and cannot scale across many VPCs/accounts without peering complexity and potential transitive routing limits.
- Cost advantage on egress in some accounts (no interface endpoint hourly charges) but introduces administrative overhead for peering maintenance and security groups cross-account considerations.

Why VPN last (short):
- Operationally heavier, higher and less predictable latency, potential for MTU fragmentation and BGP flaps depending on your gateway; treat as fallback or for on-prem datacenter handoff.

Operational notes and ops failover plan (summary):
- Primary: PrivateLink (NLB + TLS) configured with proxy header to preserve X-Forwarded-For. We'll publish a short-runbook to verify client IPs in logs and to enable mutual TLS if you require mTLS.
- Secondary (regional failover): pre-provision peering in the same region during rollout window; route weight will be managed by our smart router based on health checks to avoid blackholing sessions.
- Emergency fallback: IPSec site-to-site with clear QoS markers and keepalive; used when PrivateLink/peering are unavailable. We'll set path priorities in the Redwood routing policy to prefer PrivateLink, then peering, then VPN.

Risks to flag:
- Cross-region PrivateLink requires cross-account interface endpoints and potentially cross-region endpoints (higher egress costs).
- If you need deep packet inspection at Acme, peering will make it easier; PrivateLink terminates at the endpoint and requires your inspectors to be in-line at the endpoint VPC.
- Cost: PrivateLink has per-ENI/hour and data processing charges. We'll run a 30-day usage forecast and recommend pricing tiering/burst allowances.

Kimberly / Ben — adding you for ops and network implementation details (MTU, health-check frequencies, BGP tie-ins). I'll put a short checklist below for the implementation POC.

Checklist for POC (brief):
1) Acme creates interface endpoint service acceptance and shares service name + account id.
2) Redwood provisions NLB in our private plane, configures backend pool and proxy headers.
3) Joint traffic test with synthetic load up to expected peak (we'll include path-level tracing).
4) Validate client IPs, latency SLOs, and data egress accounting.
5) If p99 > 120ms under load, enable regional peering for that subnet and test failover.

I attached a one-page matrix (converted from your sheet) outlining perf, security, and ops effort per option. Happy to walk through live tomorrow.

—Sergio
Sergio Alvarez
Principal Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference

Attachment referenced: acme_redwood_connectivity_matrix.xlsx (converted summary)

From: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.ai>
To: sergio_alvarez@redwood.ai, ben_carter@redwood.ai
Date: 2027-11-03T14:22:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Decision: VPC peering vs PrivateLink vs Site-to-site VPN for private deployment handoff

Quick technical points from ops (copying the checklist into more detail):

MTU and fragmentation
- With VPN, MTU drops and GRE encapsulation can cause fragmentation for large payloads — set tunnel MTU to 1436 and test with our tokenized payloads. PrivateLink and peering preserve native MTU but be careful if your VPC has jumbo frames configured.

Client IP preservation
- PrivateLink + NLB + proxy preserving XFF works but requires: (a) proxy that inserts X-Forwarded-For, (b) backend service that trusts the proxy and extracts real IP. We'll include a small sidecar snippet to demonstrate.

Health checks and failover timing
- Health check frequency at 5s and 2 consecutive failures to trigger failover is a reasonable starting point for p99 objectives. Our router will failover connections per flow key (source IP/port) to avoid tearing every TCP session; note some clients will need to re-establish long-lived connections.

Logging and observability
- We'll enable connection-level traces for the POC for 72 hours and push logs to the shared drive. For auditability, we will provide signed flow records that map to request ids so you can reconcile with your audit logs.

Cost estimates (summary)
- PrivateLink (NLB-backed) — small hourly NLB + processing charge per GB. For 10 TB/month expected egress, approximate data processing = $X/GB (we'll replace with negotiated tier).
- Peering — low per-GB but cross-account route maintenance cost includes additional engineering hours.

Ben — I'll need the exact NLB timeout and proxy header format you're going to use; also, please draft a quick terraform snippet we can share with Acme for the interface endpoint acceptance flow.

—Kim
Kimberly Park
Director, Platform Ops, Redwood Inference

From: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.ai>
To: Alice Kruger <alice.kruger@acmecorp.com>, sergio_alvarez@redwood.ai
Cc: kimberly_park@redwood.ai, marissa_cole@redwood.ai
Date: 2027-11-04T15:30:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Decision: VPC peering vs PrivateLink vs Site-to-site VPN for private deployment handoff

Alice — following the POC plan, team ran a lightweight simulation in our staging region earlier today. Summary of measurable outcomes:

1) PrivateLink (NLB-backed)
- Median latency: 38ms, p99: 95ms under 4k RPS synthetic client distribution (within your p99 SLA).
- Client IP preserved in X-Forwarded-For when proxy header enabled; verified by correlating request_id => originating IP.
- Data processing costs observed: roughly 7% higher than the peering scenario for the same traffic profile due to NLB processing.

2) VPC Peering (same region)
- Median latency: 26ms, p99: 72ms for the same load. Lower cost per GB and lower tail latency, but requires additional route approval steps and IAM cross-account SG whitelists.

3) Site-to-site VPN (IPSec tunnel)
- Median latency: 110ms, p99: 200ms under synthetic load due to tunnel limits. We observed intermittent MTU fragmentation for large payloads until tunnel MTU was adjusted.

Recommendation (final):
- Proceed with PrivateLink as primary production handoff for the rollout (meets p99 SLA and provides security posture preferred by DPO).
- Simultaneously provision regional VPC peering for the main ingress subnets as a warm standby to be activated if PrivateLink issues cause p99 breaches. Peering will be the low-cost, low-latency alternative in-region.
- Use site-to-site VPN only for on-premise datacenter tie-ins and as offline emergency fallback.

Next steps (action items):
- Acme: please confirm acceptance of the PrivateLink model and sign the connectivity addendum (I attached a draft clause in the shared drive).
- Redwood (Ben/Kim): share terraform snippet and NLB/proxy config; schedule joint POC window and 72-hour observability window for the pilot.
- DPO (Acme): we will run a short mTLS proof if you want mutual auth between clients and the endpoint.

I'll formalize this into a one-page decision memo and the technical appendix with the terraform and proxy snippet.

Thanks — Ben
Ben Carter
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
